definition: Sophomoric means immature and overconfident; showing off like a juvenile.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sophomoric. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sophomoric should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The station's new morning hosts lean sophomoric — air-horn sound effects, fake accents, and a running bit about the traffic reporter's haircut.
Playful is fun without fault — the mildest rung, nowhere near sophomoric, which turns the fun into a performance of how clever the joker is.
Juvenile humor is childish for its age, yet it stops short of sophomoric: add smugness — the wink that says 'admit it, I'm brilliant' — and the line is crossed.

Callow means green and untested — a callow recruit simply has not been around long enough yet. It carries no claim of showing off. Sophomoric adds exactly that strut: half-taught cleverness performing for the room, certain it dazzles. You outgrow callow automatically; sophomoric can survive into middle age.

Immature means simply not grown up yet, and it makes no claim to cleverness. Sophomoric is immaturity with a costume on: showing off, certain the room is impressed. Any toddler is immature; it takes a little half-digested learning to be sophomoric.

For its first decade, the campus humor magazine The Griffin was proudly, almost defiantly sophomoric.
Its writers, mostly nineteen, filled each issue with fake Latin mottoes and footnotes mocking professors they had taken exactly one course from.
Every parody arrived with a flourish, as if daring the reader not to applaud.
A 1968 editor later admitted the staff 'mistook one year of learning for the whole of it, and wanted credit for the mistake.' Alumni are gentler now.
The jokes were thin, one concedes, but the confidence it took to print them was its own education.
